objective: Students will write one clear claim about a short passage and support it with one piece of quoted textual evidence introduced by a signal phrase.
hook: If you say a pizza place is the best in town, who would believe you without a single reason?
agenda: Bell ringer (5) · Mini-lesson: claim + evidence (12) · Model with the passage (8) · Practice (17) · Exit (3)
assessment: The exit ticket checks whether each student can state a defensible claim about the passage AND back it with a specific detail or quotation from the text.

script.title: Bell ringer
script.do: Project the question and have students write a one-sentence opinion with one reason.
options: Have students turn and share their reason with a partner instead of writing.
script.say: In one sentence, tell me your favorite season and one reason why.

script.title: Mini-lesson: claim + evidence
script.do: Define claim and evidence on the board, then show how a signal phrase introduces a quote.
options: Use a quick anchor chart with sentence starters instead of board notes.
script.say: A claim is an idea you can argue; evidence is the proof from the text that makes people believe you.

script.title: Model with the passage
script.do: Read the passage aloud, think aloud a claim, then quote one line using a signal phrase.
options: Cold-read a volunteer student to co-build the model claim with you.
script.say: Watch how I turn a detail from paragraph one into proof for my claim.

script.title: Practice
script.do: Students read the passage and complete the worksheet independently, then check one answer with a partner.
options: Let struggling students work in pairs on the claim task only.
script.say: Use the passage as your evidence locker, every answer should point back to the text.

script.title: Exit
script.do: Collect the exit ticket as students leave.
options: Have students post exit tickets on a wall chart by claim.
script.say: Give me one claim and one piece of evidence before you walk out.

slides.heading: Would you believe you?

notes:
## Claim + Evidence
**Claim:** A statement you can argue about (not an obvious fact). Example: "The garden changed the whole street."
**Evidence:** A specific detail or direct quotation from the text that supports the claim.
**Sentence starters:** "The passage shows...", "According to the text...", "The author writes, '...'"

**Model:** Claim: The community garden brought neighbors closer together. Evidence: The passage states, "Strangers who had never spoken now traded tomatoes over the fence." That line proves the garden created new connections between people.

worksheet.title: Claim It, Prove It: The Empty Lot
worksheet.instructions:
Read the passage below, then answer.

Read: For years the empty lot on Marigold Street was a tangle of weeds and broken glass that everyone hurried past. Then Mrs. Alvarez knocked on doors and asked if anyone wanted to grow something. That spring, neighbors hauled away trash, built wooden beds, and planted rows of peppers, sunflowers, and beans. By July the lot was bursting with color, and something else had changed. Strangers who had never spoken now traded tomatoes over the fence. Kids who used to stay inside spent afternoons watering plants and chasing butterflies. On Saturdays, families set out folding chairs and shared meals grown from the same soil. The garden did more than feed the block, it turned a forgotten corner into the heart of the neighborhood.

problems: What did the empty lot on Marigold Street look like before the garden was planted?
Who started the effort to change the lot, and what did she do first?
Name two things neighbors did together once the garden was growing.

sections.directions: Use the passage as your evidence.
problems: Analysis: How did the garden change the way neighbors treated one another? Explain using a detail from the passage.
Analysis: Why does the author call the garden "the heart of the neighborhood"? What does that phrase suggest about its importance?
Task: Write one claim about how the garden affected Marigold Street. Then support it with one quoted piece of evidence from the passage, introduced by a signal phrase.

answers: Before the garden, the lot was a tangle of weeds and broken glass that everyone hurried past.
Mrs. Alvarez started the effort; she knocked on doors and asked if anyone wanted to grow something.
Neighbors hauled away trash, built wooden beds, planted crops, traded tomatoes over the fence, and shared Saturday meals (any two).
The garden made neighbors friendlier and more connected; people who had ignored each other began interacting, since "strangers who had never spoken now traded tomatoes over the fence."

The author calls it "the heart of the neighborhood" because it became the center of community life where families gathered and shared meals, suggesting it was now the most important, life-giving place on the block.

Model: The community garden transformed Marigold Street into a close-knit community. The passage states, "Strangers who had never spoken now traded tomatoes over the fence," which shows that the garden brought isolated neighbors together.

exitTicket: Write one claim about the passage and one piece of evidence that supports it.
